dx: Primary membranous nephropathy with anti-PLA2R antibodies in a middle-aged man
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of 6 weeks of progressive swelling of both legs and foamy urine. He takes no medications. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse 76/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg. There is 3+ pitting edema to the knees. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), total cholesterol 342 mg/dL (under 200), and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urine protein excretion is 8.2 g/24 h (under 0.15). Urinalysis shows oval fat bodies and no red blood cell casts. C3 and C4 are normal. Antinuclear antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibody are negative, and age-appropriate cancer screening is normal. Serum anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibodies are positive. Kidney biopsy shows diffuse capillary wall thickening with granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops. Diagnosis: primary membranous nephropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how the immune deposits form in this patient's glomeruli?
options: Circulating immune complexes trapped in the mesangial matrix
Autoantibodies binding the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
Autoantibodies binding an antigen on the podocyte surface
Streptococcal antigens planted in the glomerular basement membrane
approach: Note the antibody that defines his disease: anti-PLA2R.
Locate the antigen: PLA2R sits on the podocyte cell membrane, on the outer (urinary) side of the basement membrane.
Conclude that circulating IgG binds the antigen in place, forming immune complexes beneath the podocytes (subepithelial).
questions.why: PLA2R is a membrane protein on podocytes. In primary membranous nephropathy, circulating IgG autoantibodies (mostly IgG4) cross the basement membrane and bind PLA2R in place, so the immune complexes form right under the podocytes. Complement is activated there, and the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) injures the podocytes, which causes heavy proteinuria. Because the deposits sit on the far side of the basement membrane from the blood, few inflammatory cells are drawn in and the urine sediment stays bland. Anti-PLA2R antibodies are found in most primary cases and are usually absent in secondary membranous disease from lupus, hepatitis B, solid tumors, or drugs such as NSAIDs.
whyNot: Trapping of circulating immune complexes in the mesangium is the pattern of IgA nephropathy and mild lupus nephritis. In membranous nephropathy the deposits lie along the capillary walls under the podocytes.
Antibodies to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen cause anti-GBM disease, with linear IgG staining and a rapidly progressive nephritic picture, not granular deposits and nephrotic syndrome.
Correct.
Planted streptococcal antigens with immune complex formation describe poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows an infection and presents with a nephritic picture and low C3.

questions.stem: Two months later, he develops left flank pain and gross hematuria. CT shows thrombus in the left renal vein. A continuous heparin infusion is started, but the activated partial thromboplastin time rises only slightly despite repeated dose increases. Which of the following best explains his poor response to heparin?
options: Urinary loss of the protease inhibitor that heparin activates
Antibodies against complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4
Hepatic underproduction of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
A factor V variant that resists cleavage by activated protein C
approach: Recall that heparin has no anticoagulant effect on its own; it works by binding antithrombin.
Ask what nephrotic syndrome does to antithrombin: it is about the size of albumin, so it leaks into the urine.
Conclude that low plasma antithrombin explains both the renal vein thrombosis and the heparin resistance.
questions.why: Antithrombin is a serine protease inhibitor (a serpin) made in the liver. It inactivates thrombin and factor Xa, and heparin binds it and speeds this reaction enormously. Antithrombin is a small plasma protein close in size to albumin, so it is lost in the urine in nephrotic syndrome. With little antithrombin left, heparin has nothing to work through, and the activated partial thromboplastin time barely changes. The same loss tips the balance toward clotting, while larger procoagulant proteins such as fibrinogen are kept in the plasma and made in greater amounts by the liver. This is why renal vein thrombosis is a classic complication of nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy.
whyNot: Correct.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia causes a falling platelet count and new clots about 5 to 10 days after heparin is started. It does not stop heparin from prolonging the clotting time.
Low vitamin K-dependent factors, as with warfarin or liver failure, prolong clotting times. They would not make heparin less effective.
Factor V Leiden raises the risk of venous thrombosis, but heparin still acts normally through antithrombin, so the clotting time responds as expected.

questions.stem: Before the CT, Doppler ultrasonography of the left renal hilum shows three tubular structures: a thin-walled vessel with low-velocity continuous flow, a vessel with pulsatile high-velocity flow, and a structure without flow that is continuous with the ureter. Which of the following gives the order of these structures from anterior to posterior?
options: Pulsatile vessel, nonpulsatile vessel, structure without flow
Structure without flow, pulsatile vessel, nonpulsatile vessel
Nonpulsatile vessel, structure without flow, pulsatile vessel
Nonpulsatile vessel, pulsatile vessel, structure without flow
approach: Identify each structure: continuous low-velocity flow is the renal vein, pulsatile flow is the renal artery, and the structure without flow that leads to the ureter is the renal pelvis.
Recall the hilar order from front to back: vein, artery, pelvis.
Translate back into the descriptions given.
questions.why: At the renal hilum the main structures lie in a fixed order from anterior to posterior: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis. The vein is the most anterior and the pelvis the most posterior. The whole kidney, with its hilar structures, sits inside the fibrous capsule, then perirenal fat, then renal fascia, then pararenal fat. In this patient, the left renal vein is the vessel at risk of thrombosis because of urinary antithrombin loss.
whyNot: This places the renal artery in front of the vein. The vein is the most anterior hilar structure.
This reverses the true order and puts the renal pelvis in front. The pelvis is the most posterior structure.
This puts the renal pelvis between the two vessels. The artery lies between the vein in front and the pelvis behind.
Correct.

questions.stem: Membranous nephropathy is also one of the patterns of lupus nephritis. Compared with membranous lupus nephritis, the most common and most severe class of lupus nephritis is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Subepithelial deposits with heavy proteinuria and a bland sediment
Subendothelial deposits with red cell casts and hypertension
Linear IgG along the basement membrane with lung hemorrhage
Mesangial IgA deposits with normal complement levels
approach: Name the most common and most severe class: diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis.
Recall where its immune complexes sit: subendothelial, on the blood side of the basement membrane.
Predict the result: inflammation and a nephritic picture, unlike the nephrotic picture of membranous disease.
questions.why: Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is the most common and most severe class. Immune complexes of DNA and anti-DNA antibodies deposit under the endothelium, where they are exposed to the blood. Complement activation there recruits neutrophils and monocytes and drives cell proliferation, so patients have hematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, and falling GFR. Large subendothelial deposits thicken the capillary walls into wire loops. Serum C3 and C4 are low and anti-dsDNA titers are high. Membranous lupus nephritis, like this patient's lesion, has subepithelial deposits and presents as nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot: This describes membranous disease, either primary or the membranous class of lupus nephritis. The most severe class is proliferative and nephritic.
Correct.
Linear IgG with lung hemorrhage is anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), a type II hypersensitivity, not lupus.
Mesangial IgA with normal complement is IgA nephropathy. Active lupus nephritis lowers both C3 and C4.

dx: Dense deposit disease (C3 glomerulopathy) with C3 nephritic factor in a teenager
case: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of 2 weeks of dark brown urine and swelling around her eyes. She has had no recent sore throat or skin infection. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse 84/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL (0.5 to 1.0). Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, and urine protein is 2.6 g/24 h (under 0.15). Serum C3 is 24 mg/dL (90 to 180), and C4 is 22 mg/dL (10 to 40). Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers are normal. C3 nephritic factor is detected. Kidney biopsy shows mesangial proliferation, double contours of the capillary walls, bright C3 staining with little immunoglobulin, and dense ribbon-like deposits within the basement membrane on electron microscopy. Diagnosis: dense deposit disease (C3 glomerulopathy).

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her low serum C3 concentration?
options: Circulating immune complexes that activate C1q in the classical pathway
An autoantibody that stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase
Inherited deficiency of the C1 esterase inhibitor that regulates C1
Reduced hepatic synthesis of C3 from impaired liver function
approach: Read the complement pattern: C3 is low and C4 is normal, so the classical pathway is not being consumed.
Name the antibody in the case: C3 nephritic factor.
Recall its target: the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), which it protects from breakdown.
questions.why: C3 nephritic factor is an IgG autoantibody that binds C3bBb, the alternative pathway C3 convertase, and shields it from inactivation by factor H. The convertase keeps cleaving C3 in the fluid phase, so C3 is used up and stays low. C4 is used only by the classical and lectin pathways, so it stays normal. C3 breakdown products collect in the glomerular basement membrane as the dense deposits seen on electron microscopy, and the glomeruli show the membranoproliferative pattern with double contours. Immune complex membranoproliferative disease, by contrast, is linked to hepatitis B and C.
whyNot: Classical pathway activation by immune complexes consumes C4 as well as C3, as in lupus nephritis or cryoglobulinemic disease. Her C4 is normal.
Correct.
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema with low C4. It does not cause glomerulonephritis with low C3 and normal C4.
Liver failure would lower many plasma proteins, including C4, and would not explain C3 nephritic factor or C3 deposits in the glomeruli.

questions.stem: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis was considered when she first presented. Which of the following courses of serum complement is most likely in her disease and best distinguishes it from poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
options: C3 and C4 both normal at onset and at 12 weeks
C3 low at onset and back to normal by 8 weeks
C3 and C4 both low at onset and at 12 weeks
C3 low at onset and still low at 12 weeks
approach: Note that both diseases lower C3 with a normal C4, so a single measurement cannot separate them.
Recall the time course: poststreptococcal C3 recovers within about 6 to 8 weeks once the antigen is cleared.
Apply it: C3 nephritic factor keeps the convertase active, so her C3 stays low for months.
questions.why: In poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, immune complexes activate complement for a short time. C3 falls and then returns to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks. In membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and C3 glomerulopathy, the drive on complement continues, so C3 stays low long after 8 weeks. A low C3 that persists is a classic clue to look beyond poststreptococcal disease. Low C3 and C4 together point to classical pathway use, as in lupus nephritis, while normal complement fits IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, and ANCA vasculitis.
whyNot: Normal complement throughout fits IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, or ANCA vasculitis. Her C3 is already low.
This is the expected course of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, the disease being excluded.
Persistently low C3 and C4 suggest classical pathway activation, as in lupus nephritis. Her C4 is normal.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three months later, her creatinine rises to 3.6 mg/dL over 2 weeks. A repeat biopsy shows crescents in 60% of glomeruli. Which of the following resident cells proliferate to form these crescents?
options: Parietal epithelial cells lining Bowman capsule
Intraglomerular mesangial cells in the capillary tuft
Fenestrated endothelial cells of the glomerular capillaries
Granular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole
approach: Recognize rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis: a fast rise in creatinine with crescents in most glomeruli.
Recall where a crescent sits: in Bowman space, between the capillary tuft and Bowman capsule.
Recall what normally lines the outer wall of Bowman space: simple squamous parietal epithelial cells, which proliferate after fibrin leaks into the space.
questions.why: Bowman capsule has two layers. The visceral layer is the podocytes wrapped around the capillary loops, and the parietal layer is a simple squamous epithelium lining the outer wall of Bowman space. When severe injury breaks the capillary walls, fibrinogen leaks into Bowman space and forms fibrin. Fibrin and cytokines drive the parietal epithelial cells to proliferate, and monocytes and macrophages move in, forming a crescent that compresses the capillary tuft. Over weeks, cellular crescents are replaced by collagen. Crescentic disease is sorted by immunofluorescence into linear (anti-GBM), granular (immune complex), and pauci-immune (ANCA) types.
whyNot: Correct.
Mesangial cells proliferate inside the capillary tuft, as in IgA nephropathy and membranoproliferative disease. They do not fill Bowman space.
Endothelial cells swell and proliferate inside the capillary lumens in diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, such as poststreptococcal disease. They do not form crescents.
Granular (juxtaglomerular) cells sit in the afferent arteriole wall and secrete renin. They lie outside Bowman space and do not form crescents.

questions.stem: Her 8-year-old cousin develops swelling around the eyes and cola-colored urine 3 weeks after impetigo. Serum C3 is low and C4 is normal. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of his glomerular injury?
options: Bacteria invading glomerular capillaries during bacteremia
Bacterial exotoxin killing glomerular endothelial cells directly
Immune complexes containing streptococcal antigens in glomeruli
Autoantibodies to the noncollagenous domain of type IV collagen
approach: Recognize poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: a nephritic picture weeks after a group A streptococcal skin infection, with low C3.
Use the latent period as the clue: the delay is the time needed to make antibodies.
Conclude that the injury is a type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity, not infection of the kidney.
questions.why: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows infection with nephritogenic strains of group A streptococci after a latent period of about 1 to 4 weeks, often longer after skin infection than after pharyngitis. During that time the child makes antibodies against streptococcal antigens. Antigen and antibody form immune complexes in the glomeruli, seen as granular IgG and C3 and as subepithelial humps on electron microscopy. Complement activation lowers C3 and recruits neutrophils, causing hematuria, edema, and hypertension. The kidney itself is sterile, and most children recover fully.
whyNot: The kidney is not infected in poststreptococcal disease. Cultures of the kidney are sterile, and the delay after the infection points to an immune mechanism.
Direct toxin injury to endothelium describes Shiga toxin in hemolytic uremic syndrome after bloody diarrhea, not glomerulonephritis after impetigo.
Correct.
Antibodies to type IV collagen cause anti-GBM disease, with linear IgG staining and normal complement. It does not follow a skin infection.

dx: Microscopic polyangiitis with MPO-ANCA pulmonary-renal syndrome
case: A 67-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 3 weeks of fatigue, low-grade fever, and cough with blood-streaked sputum, and 2 days of decreased urine output. She has no sinus or ear symptoms. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse 98/min, respirations 24/min, and blood pressure 156/92 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 4.8 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), up from 0.9 mg/dL 2 months ago, and BUN is 62 mg/dL (7 to 20). Urinalysis shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts. Chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy alveolar opacities. Myeloperoxidase ANCA is positive, and proteinase 3 ANCA and anti-GBM antibodies are negative. C3 and C4 are normal. Kidney biopsy shows necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis with little or no immunoglobulin or complement and no granulomas. Diagnosis: microscopic polyangiitis with pulmonary-renal syndrome.

questions.stem: Polyarteritis nodosa was briefly considered because of her hypertension and constitutional symptoms. Which of the following findings in this patient argues most strongly against polyarteritis nodosa?
options: Normal serum C3 and C4 concentrations
Fever and progressive fatigue
Blood pressure of 156/92 mm Hg
Red blood cell casts in the urine
approach: Recall the vessel size in polyarteritis nodosa: medium-sized muscular arteries, sparing capillaries.
Ask which finding requires inflammation of glomerular capillaries: red blood cell casts.
Conclude that glomerulonephritis points to a small-vessel vasculitis such as microscopic polyangiitis.
questions.why: Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries. It spares capillaries, venules, glomeruli, and usually the lungs. Its renal disease comes from inflamed renal and interlobar arteries, with microaneurysms, infarcts, hematuria without red cell casts, and renin-driven hypertension, and it is ANCA negative. Red cell casts mean the glomerular capillaries are inflamed, which places her disease among the small-vessel vasculitides. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA, no granulomas) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA, necrotizing granulomas of the airways) both cause glomerulonephritis with lung capillaritis.
whyNot: Complement is normal in both polyarteritis nodosa and ANCA vasculitis, so it does not separate them.
Fever and fatigue occur in nearly all systemic vasculitides, including polyarteritis nodosa.
Hypertension is common in polyarteritis nodosa from renin release by ischemic kidney tissue, so it does not argue against it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.31 (7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 29 mm Hg (35 to 45), and HCO3- 14 mEq/L (22 to 28). Which of the following best describes her acid-base status?
options: Metabolic acidosis with a superimposed respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with a superimposed respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis with appropriate renal compensation
approach: Identify the primary process: low pH with low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis.
Apply Winters formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2 (27 to 31 mm Hg).
Compare: the measured PaCO2 of 29 falls in the range, so compensation is appropriate.
questions.why: The low pH and low bicarbonate show a primary metabolic acidosis. The lungs respond by hyperventilating, and Winters formula predicts how far the PaCO2 should fall: 1.5 times the bicarbonate plus 8, plus or minus 2. Here that is 27 to 31 mm Hg, and her PaCO2 is 29, so this is a simple metabolic acidosis with the expected respiratory response. A PaCO2 below 27 would mean an added respiratory alkalosis, as can happen with lung disease or sepsis. A PaCO2 above 31 would mean an added respiratory acidosis.
whyNot: An added respiratory acidosis would leave the PaCO2 above the predicted 27 to 31 mm Hg. Hers is in range.
Correct.
An added respiratory alkalosis would push the PaCO2 below 27 mm Hg. Hers is within the predicted range.
A primary respiratory alkalosis would raise the pH. Her pH is low, so the primary problem is acidosis.

questions.stem: Renal ultrasonography shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. Which of the following best classifies her acute kidney injury?
options: Prerenal, because her BUN rose more than her creatinine
Postrenal, because urine outflow from both kidneys is obstructed
Intrinsic, from glomerular inflammation shown by red cell casts
Intrinsic, from tubular necrosis shown by muddy brown casts
approach: Calculate the BUN to creatinine ratio: 62 divided by 4.8 is about 13, which is not above 20.
Exclude postrenal injury: there is no hydronephrosis.
Localize the intrinsic injury with the urine sediment: dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts come from the glomerulus.
questions.why: Acute kidney injury is sorted into prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal causes. A BUN to creatinine ratio above 20 suggests prerenal injury, because low flow lets the tubules reabsorb more urea. Her ratio is about 13, which fits intrinsic disease. Normal ultrasonography without hydronephrosis rules out a postrenal cause. Red cell casts form when red cells leak through inflamed glomeruli and are molded in the tubules, so they place the injury in the glomerulus. The fractional excretion of sodium can stay low early in glomerulonephritis because the tubules still work, so the sediment is the more reliable clue here.
whyNot: A BUN to creatinine ratio above 20 suggests prerenal injury. Hers is about 13, and her red cell casts point to the kidney itself.
Postrenal injury needs obstruction of both outflow tracts, or of a single functioning kidney, and usually shows hydronephrosis. Her ultrasonography is normal.
Correct.
Muddy brown granular casts mark acute tubular necrosis. Her urine shows red cell casts, which come from glomerular inflammation.

questions.stem: Serum studies show sodium 138 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 14 mEq/L. Serum glucose is 96 mg/dL, lactate is 1.2 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), and serum ketones are negative. The normal anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her acidosis?
options: Retention of sulfate, phosphate, and organic anions
Loss of bicarbonate from the gastrointestinal tract
Accumulation of acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate
Failure of distal tubular hydrogen ion secretion
approach: Calculate the anion gap: 138 minus (104 plus 14) equals 20 mEq/L, which is high.
Exclude the other high gap causes using the data: lactate is normal and ketones are negative.
Conclude that her severe renal failure is retaining unmeasured anions (uremic acidosis).
questions.why: The anion gap is sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate, here 20 mEq/L, which is high. A high gap means an unmeasured acid anion has replaced bicarbonate. Lactate is normal, ketones are absent, and there is no history of a toxic alcohol or salicylate, so the cause is uremia. When GFR falls severely, the kidney can neither excrete the daily acid load nor filter anions such as sulfate, phosphate, and urate, and these build up in the blood. Diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis lose bicarbonate and raise chloride instead, giving a normal anion gap.
whyNot: Correct.
Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, as in diarrhea, causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis. Her gap is high.
Ketoacids raise the anion gap in diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis, but her glucose is normal and ketones are negative.
Distal renal tubular acidosis causes a normal anion gap acidosis with a high urine pH, not a high gap acidosis.

dx: Polyarteritis nodosa with renal artery microaneurysms and renal infarction
case: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of sudden severe left flank pain and red urine that began 4 hours ago. For 3 months he has had fever, muscle aches, a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss, abdominal pain after meals, and weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse 96/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 168/102 mm Hg. Hepatitis B surface antigen is positive. Serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urinalysis shows red blood cells without red cell casts and trace protein. ANCA testing is negative. Contrast CT shows a wedge-shaped, nonenhancing region in the left kidney. Angiography shows multiple small aneurysms of the renal and mesenteric arteries. Diagnosis: polyarteritis nodosa with renal infarction.

questions.stem: If the infarcted region were examined grossly 2 days after onset, it would appear pale. Which of the following best explains this appearance?
options: A single arterial supply to a solid, dense organ
A dual blood supply that lets blood flow into the dead tissue
Obstruction of venous outflow with backup of blood
Liquefaction of the tissue by neutrophil enzymes
approach: Identify the cause of the infarct: arterial occlusion, here from thrombosis of an inflamed medium-sized artery.
Recall what decides pale versus red infarcts: the type of blood supply and the density of the tissue.
Apply it: the kidney has end arteries and dense tissue, so little blood enters the dead area.
questions.why: Pale (white) infarcts follow arterial occlusion in solid organs with a single end-arterial supply, such as the kidney, heart, and spleen. No second supply refills the territory, and the dense tissue limits bleeding in from the edges, so the dead area looks pale. Red (hemorrhagic) infarcts occur with venous occlusion, in loose tissue with a dual supply such as the lung and small bowel, or after reperfusion. The kidney undergoes coagulative necrosis, producing the wedge-shaped infarct with flank pain and hematuria. In polyarteritis nodosa, transmural necrotizing inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis weakens medium-sized arteries, causing aneurysms and thrombosis.
whyNot: Correct.
A dual blood supply lets blood seep into the dead tissue and produces a red infarct, as in the lung. The kidney lacks this.
Venous obstruction causes congestion and a hemorrhagic infarct, as in testicular torsion or renal vein thrombosis. His infarct is from arterial disease.
Liquefactive necrosis is typical of the brain and of abscesses. Ischemic kidney tissue undergoes coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: The angiogram shows complete occlusion of the posterior segmental branch of the left renal artery. Which of the following best describes the tissue most likely to be infarcted?
options: The entire left kidney, because the segmental arteries share one territory
None, because adjacent segmental arteries provide collateral flow
Only the posterior segment, because segmental arteries do not anastomose
Only the medulla, because the cortex receives capsular collateral flow
approach: Recall how the renal artery branches at the hilum: into segmental arteries, each supplying its own segment.
Recall that segmental arteries have no meaningful anastomoses, so they act as end arteries.
Predict infarction limited to the territory of the blocked branch.
questions.why: The renal artery divides near the hilum into segmental arteries, usually five (superior, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, and posterior). Each supplies its own segment, and there are no useful anastomoses between them, so each behaves as an end artery. The same is true of the interlobar arteries further downstream. When one segmental artery is blocked, the tissue it supplies dies, and the rest of the kidney is spared. Capsular vessels keep only a thin rim of outer cortex alive at the edge of a renal infarct.
whyNot: Each segmental artery has its own territory, so a single branch occlusion does not infarct the whole kidney. That would need occlusion of the main renal artery.
Segmental arteries do not supply one another, so no collateral flow rescues the blocked segment.
Correct.
Capsular vessels supply only a thin subcapsular rim. The cortex of the blocked segment dies along with its medulla.

questions.stem: His hypertension is attributed to renin release from ischemic kidney tissue downstream of the diseased arteries. Which of the following signals most directly stimulates renin release in this setting?
options: Increased sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa
Reduced stretch of juxtaglomerular cells in afferent arterioles
Increased atrial natriuretic peptide acting on juxtaglomerular cells
Decreased beta-1 adrenergic stimulation of granular cells
approach: Recall the three stimuli for renin release: low perfusion pressure, low NaCl at the macula densa, and beta-1 sympathetic input.
Identify the one created by narrowed, aneurysmal arteries: low pressure in the afferent arterioles downstream.
Conclude that the juxtaglomerular cells sense less stretch and release renin.
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole. They act as baroreceptors, releasing renin when perfusion pressure falls and the arteriole wall is stretched less. Renin is also released when the macula densa senses low NaCl and when beta-1 sympathetic nerves fire. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which ACE converts to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles, increases proximal sodium reabsorption, and stimulates aldosterone, ADH, and thirst, all of which raise blood pressure. Atrial natriuretic peptide opposes this system.
whyNot: High NaCl at the macula densa suppresses renin release. Low NaCl delivery stimulates it.
Correct.
Atrial natriuretic peptide inhibits renin release and promotes sodium excretion, so it would lower blood pressure.
Beta-1 stimulation increases renin release. Less sympathetic input would lower renin.

questions.stem: Renal artery stenosis is another cause of renin-dependent hypertension. In a patient with severe stenosis of both renal arteries, starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is most likely to cause which of the following?
options: A rise in GFR from dilation of the afferent arterioles
A fall in GFR from constriction of the afferent arterioles
No change in GFR because of tubuloglomerular feedback
A fall in GFR from dilation of the efferent arterioles
approach: Recognize that low perfusion behind both stenoses drives high renin and angiotensin II levels.
Recall that angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, holding up glomerular capillary pressure.
Predict that removing angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole, so glomerular pressure and GFR fall.
questions.why: In renal artery stenosis, low pressure beyond the narrowing triggers renin release, and angiotensin II raises systemic pressure. Inside the kidney, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, which keeps glomerular capillary pressure and GFR up despite poor inflow. When both kidneys depend on this, an ACE inhibitor removes the efferent constriction, glomerular pressure drops, and GFR falls, with a rise in creatinine. Atherosclerotic stenosis affects older adults at the ostium or proximal artery, while fibromuscular dysplasia affects young women with a string of beads appearance. Both may cause an abdominal bruit and atrophy of the affected kidney.
whyNot: ACE inhibitors act mainly on the efferent arteriole, and the result in bilateral stenosis is a fall in GFR, not a rise.
Removing angiotensin II does not constrict the afferent arteriole. The GFR falls because the efferent arteriole relaxes.
Autoregulation cannot keep up GFR when inflow is severely limited and the efferent constriction that was holding it up is removed.
Correct.

topics: Angiotensin II and the efferent arteriole

dx: Thin basement membrane disease with familial microscopic hematuria
case: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up of microscopic hematuria found on a routine examination. She has no symptoms. Urinalyses on three occasions show 10 to 20 red blood cells/hpf (0 to 2), many of them dysmorphic, with no casts and no protein. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Hearing and eye examinations are normal. Her 56-year-old mother and her brother have microscopic hematuria with normal kidney function. Kidney biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence. Electron microscopy shows uniformly thin glomerular basement membranes of about 190 nm (adult normal about 300 to 400 nm). Genetic testing shows a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in COL4A4. Diagnosis: thin basement membrane disease.

questions.stem: Her husband also has persistent microscopic hematuria and carries a different heterozygous loss-of-function variant in COL4A4. A child who inherits both parents' variants is most likely to develop which of the following?
options: Isolated microscopic hematuria with a thin basement membrane
X-linked Alport syndrome with milder disease in girls
Autosomal recessive Alport syndrome with renal failure
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with liver cysts
approach: Recall that the glomerular basement membrane collagen is a trimer of alpha-3, alpha-4, and alpha-5 chains, and COL4A4 is on an autosome.
One defective COL4A4 allele leaves enough normal network for a thin but working membrane.
Two defective alleles leave no functional alpha-3/alpha-4/alpha-5 network, which is autosomal recessive Alport syndrome.
questions.why: Type IV collagen in the mature glomerular basement membrane is built from alpha-3, alpha-4, and alpha-5 chains. COL4A3 and COL4A4 are on chromosome 2, and COL4A5 is on the X chromosome. A single defective COL4A3 or COL4A4 allele usually causes thin basement membrane disease, with lifelong hematuria and normal kidney function in most people. When a child inherits defective alleles from both parents, no normal network can form, and the result is autosomal recessive Alport syndrome. It causes hematuria progressing to renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye lesions, and it affects boys and girls equally. Each child of this couple has a 1 in 4 chance of this outcome.
whyNot: One defective allele gives thin basement membrane disease. A child with both parents' variants has no normal allele and develops Alport syndrome.
X-linked Alport syndrome comes from COL4A5 variants on the X chromosome. These variants are in COL4A4, an autosomal gene.
Correct.
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease comes from PKD1 or PKD2 variants, not from type IV collagen genes.

questions.stem: Alport syndrome is the main condition to exclude in a patient like her. Which of the following electron microscopy findings would indicate Alport syndrome rather than thin basement membrane disease?
options: Subepithelial humps along the outer basement membrane
Ribbon-like dense deposits within the lamina densa
Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes alone
Irregular thinning and splitting of the lamina densa
approach: Recall that both diseases come from defective type IV collagen, so both can show thin segments.
Recall the extra change in Alport syndrome: the abnormal network breaks down into split, layered lamina densa.
Choose the finding that shows splitting, the basket-weave pattern.
questions.why: In thin basement membrane disease the membrane is uniformly thin but otherwise normal. In Alport syndrome the defective collagen network cannot hold its structure, so the basement membrane becomes irregularly thin in some places and thick in others, and the lamina densa splits into layers with a basket-weave appearance. Clinically, Alport syndrome causes hematuria that progresses to renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus, because the same collagen chains are found in the cochlea and lens capsule. Males with the X-linked form have the most severe disease.
whyNot: Subepithelial humps are the immune deposits of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, not a collagen defect.
Dense ribbon-like deposits in the lamina densa define dense deposit disease, a C3 glomerulopathy.
Foot process effacement alone is the electron microscopy finding of minimal change disease.
Correct.

questions.stem: IgA nephropathy is another common cause of glomerular hematuria in young adults. In a patient with IgA nephropathy, which of the following combinations is most likely?
options: Hematuria 1 to 2 days after a sore throat, with normal C3
Hematuria 2 to 3 weeks after a sore throat, with low C3
Hematuria 1 to 2 days after a sore throat, with low C3 and C4
Hematuria 2 to 3 weeks after a sore throat, with normal C3
approach: Recall the timing in IgA nephropathy: visible hematuria starts within a day or two of a mucosal infection.
Recall the complement level: serum C3 is normal.
Contrast poststreptococcal disease: a latent period of weeks and a low C3.
questions.why: IgA nephropathy comes from abnormal IgA1 that forms immune complexes and deposits in the mesangium. A mucosal infection boosts IgA production, so episodes of gross hematuria start within 1 to 2 days of a sore throat or gastrointestinal infection. Serum complement stays normal. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis needs time for antibodies to form, so it appears 1 to 3 weeks or more after the infection and lowers C3. Low C3 and C4 together suggest lupus nephritis.
whyNot: Correct.
A latent period of weeks with low C3 is the pattern of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Low C3 and C4 suggest classical pathway activation, as in lupus nephritis. IgA nephropathy has normal complement.
IgA nephropathy hematuria comes within days of the infection, not after a latent period of weeks.

questions.stem: Percutaneous kidney biopsy is performed with her lying prone, and the needle is aimed at the lower pole of the kidney rather than the upper pole. Which of the following best explains this choice?
options: The upper pole is covered posteriorly by the psoas major muscle
The upper pole lies against the diaphragm and pleural recess
The lower pole lies above the 12th rib, which shields the needle
The upper pole is intraperitoneal and covered by the liver
approach: Recall the vertical position of the kidneys: about T12 to L3, with the right lower than the left because of the liver.
Recall the posterior relations of the upper pole: the diaphragm and 12th rib, with the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura behind the diaphragm.
Conclude that a needle into the upper pole risks entering the pleura, so the lower pole is safer.
questions.why: The kidneys lie in the retroperitoneum from about T12 to L3, and the right kidney sits slightly lower because the liver is above it. Behind the upper pole lie the diaphragm and the 12th rib, and behind the diaphragm the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura extends down to about the 12th rib. A needle aimed at the upper pole can therefore cause a pneumothorax. The lower pole lies on the quadratus lumborum laterally and the psoas major medially, below the ribs and away from the pleura and the large hilar vessels.
whyNot: The psoas major lies medial and posterior to the lower part of the kidney, and the needle approaches lateral to it. It is not the reason for avoiding the upper pole.
Correct.
The lower pole lies below the 12th rib, which is what allows a needle to reach it between the rib and the iliac crest.
Both kidneys are retroperitoneal. The liver lies anterior to the upper right kidney, not behind it in the needle path.

dx: Minimal change disease in an adult with Hodgkin lymphoma
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of swelling of his face and legs. For 2 months he has had night sweats, itching, and a painless lump in his neck. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse 82/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. There is generalized pitting edema and a 3-cm nontender supraclavicular lymph node. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5), total cholesterol 384 mg/dL (under 200), and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urine protein is 9.6 g/24 h (under 0.15), mostly albumin, with no red blood cells. C3 and C4 are normal. Lymph node biopsy shows CD15- and CD30-positive Reed-Sternberg cells. Kidney biopsy shows normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence and Congo red staining, and diffuse foot process effacement. Diagnosis: minimal change disease associated with Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: His proteinuria resolves completely after chemotherapy for the lymphoma. Which of the following best explains the link between his two diseases?
options: Immune complexes of tumor antigen deposited beneath the podocytes
Circulating factors from abnormal T cells that injure podocytes
Monoclonal light chain fibrils deposited in the glomerular mesangium
Infiltration of the renal interstitium by lymphoma cells
approach: Use the biopsy: no immune deposits, no amyloid, and no tumor cells, only foot process effacement.
Recall the leading explanation for minimal change disease: immune dysregulation releases circulating factors that injure podocytes.
Connect it to the lymphoma: Hodgkin lymphoma disturbs T-cell function, and treating it removes the source.
questions.why: Minimal change disease shows no immune deposits on immunofluorescence or electron microscopy. The injury is thought to come from immune dysregulation, with T cells and related immune cells releasing circulating factors that damage podocytes and cause foot process effacement and selective albuminuria. Hodgkin lymphoma disturbs T-cell function and cytokine release, which explains why minimal change disease can appear with it and remit when the lymphoma is treated. In children, minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome and responds well to corticosteroids, which suppress this immune activity.
whyNot: Tumor antigen immune complexes beneath podocytes cause membranous nephropathy, linked to solid tumors such as lung and colon carcinoma. His immunofluorescence is negative.
Correct.
Light chain deposits cause AL amyloidosis or light chain deposition disease. His Congo red stain is negative and the glomeruli are normal by light microscopy.
His biopsy shows no lymphoma cells, and interstitial infiltration would cause tubular injury rather than heavy selective albuminuria.

questions.stem: Suppose his proteinuria had persisted despite 16 weeks of high-dose corticosteroids and successful treatment of the lymphoma. A repeat kidney biopsy would most likely show which of the following?
options: Sclerosis of parts of some glomeruli with hyaline deposits
Nodular mesangial expansion with hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Diffuse capillary wall thickening with basement membrane spikes
Crescents of proliferating cells filling Bowman space
approach: Recognize steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in an adult whose first biopsy looked like minimal change disease.
Recall that focal segmental glomerulosclerosis affects only some glomeruli and can be missed on a small first biopsy.
Recall its lesion: segmental sclerosis with hyalinosis in some glomeruli, from podocyte injury.
questions.why: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis affects only some glomeruli (focal) and only part of each affected tuft (segmental), where the capillaries collapse into sclerosis with hyaline deposits. Because it is focal, a first biopsy may sample only normal glomeruli and look like minimal change disease. Both diseases start with podocyte injury, but focal segmental glomerulosclerosis responds poorly to steroids and often progresses. Secondary causes include HIV infection (collapsing variant), heroin use, sickle cell disease, and obesity.
whyNot: Correct.
Nodular mesangial expansion with hyaline arteriolosclerosis is diabetic nephropathy. He has no diabetes.
Capillary wall thickening with spikes is membranous nephropathy, which would have shown granular IgG and C3 on his first biopsy.
Crescents mark rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with a nephritic picture and falling GFR rather than isolated nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: His serum sodium is 131 mEq/L (135 to 145). Nonosmotic release of antidiuretic hormone contributes to his water retention. Which of the following best describes how this hormone reduces water excretion?
options: V1 receptor calcium signaling that constricts vascular smooth muscle
Mineralocorticoid receptor activation that increases ENaC synthesis
Inhibition of Na-K-2Cl cotransport in the thick ascending limb
V2 receptor signaling that inserts aquaporin-2 in principal cells
approach: Identify the hormone and its renal receptor: ADH acts on V2 receptors of collecting duct principal cells.
Trace the signal: Gs, cAMP, and protein kinase A move aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane.
Predict the effect: more water is reabsorbed, urine is concentrated, and serum sodium falls.
questions.why: ADH binds V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of collecting duct principal cells. The receptor acts through Gs to raise cAMP, and protein kinase A moves vesicles containing aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. Water then enters the cell through aquaporin-2 and leaves through basolateral aquaporins into the hypertonic medulla. ADH also raises urea permeability in the inner medullary collecting duct, which helps build the medullary gradient. In nephrotic syndrome, a low effective circulating volume can trigger ADH release despite a low plasma osmolality, which dilutes the serum sodium.
whyNot: V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle raise intracellular calcium and cause vasoconstriction. They do not control water reabsorption.
Aldosterone acts on mineralocorticoid receptors to increase ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase. This retains sodium rather than free water.
Loop diuretics inhibit Na-K-2Cl cotransport. ADH does not, and inhibiting it would reduce the ability to concentrate urine.
Correct.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of his biopsy shows loss of the normal regular spacing between podocyte foot processes. Which of the following structures normally bridges the narrow gaps between adjacent foot processes and restricts albumin filtration?
options: Tight junctions sealed by claudins
Desmosomes linked by desmoglein
Slit diaphragms containing nephrin
Gap junctions formed by connexins
approach: Identify the injured cells: podocytes, the outer layer of the filtration barrier.
Recall the junction unique to their foot processes: the slit diaphragm, built from nephrin and related proteins.
Predict that effacement disrupts the slit diaphragms, so albumin crosses.
questions.why: The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, a basement membrane of type IV collagen with negatively charged heparan sulfate, and podocytes. Podocyte foot processes interlock, and the gaps between them are spanned by slit diaphragms, a thin protein bridge made largely of nephrin with podocin as a partner. The slit diaphragm is a key size barrier to albumin. When foot processes efface, as in minimal change disease, the slit diaphragms are lost or displaced and albumin leaks into the urine. Mutations in the nephrin gene cause congenital nephrotic syndrome.
whyNot: Tight junctions with claudins seal epithelia such as the thick ascending limb, where claudins form the paracellular path for magnesium and calcium. They do not join podocyte foot processes.
Desmosomes anchor cells to each other for mechanical strength, as in the epidermis. They are not the filtration slit.
Correct.
Gap junctions let ions and small molecules pass between neighboring cells. They do not span the filtration slits.

dx: Sickle cell disease nephropathy with isosthenuria in an adolescent
case: A 15-year-old boy with sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought to the physician because of bedwetting and waking 3 times each night to urinate. He drinks large amounts of water. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse 80/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 108/64 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 142 mEq/L (135 to 145), and creatinine is 0.4 mg/dL (0.5 to 1.0). Urinalysis shows 5 to 10 red blood cells/hpf (0 to 2), and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 48 mg/g (under 30). After 12 hours of water restriction, urine osmolality is 310 mOsm/kg (expected above 800), and it does not rise after desmopressin. Diagnosis: sickle cell nephropathy with isosthenuria.

questions.stem: Sickling occurs mainly in the vasa recta of his renal medulla, where oxygen tension is low. Which of the following molecular properties of his hemoglobin most directly allows this sickling?
options: Lysine in place of glutamate that promotes intracellular crystals
Reduced synthesis of structurally normal beta-globin chains
Heme iron oxidized to the ferric state that cannot bind oxygen
Valine in place of glutamate that binds adjacent deoxyhemoglobin
approach: Recall the HbS mutation: glutamate is replaced by valine at position 6 of beta-globin.
Recall what the valine does: when HbS is deoxygenated, the hydrophobic valine binds a pocket on a neighboring HbS molecule, so the molecules polymerize.
Link to the medulla: low oxygen, high osmolality, and low pH all increase deoxygenated HbS and its concentration, favoring polymers.
questions.why: In HbS, a single base change replaces glutamate, a charged amino acid, with valine, a hydrophobic one, at position 6 of the beta chain. When HbS gives up oxygen, the valine fits into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring deoxygenated HbS molecule, and long rigid polymers form that distort the red cell. The renal medulla is ideal for this: oxygen tension is low because oxygen short-circuits across the hairpin vasa recta, the hypertonic interstitium pulls water out of red cells and concentrates their HbS, the acidic pH lowers oxygen affinity, and flow is slow. Sickled cells block the vasa recta, causing hematuria, papillary necrosis, and isosthenuria.
whyNot: Lysine in place of glutamate is HbC, which forms crystals and causes mild hemolysis but does not polymerize like HbS.
Reduced synthesis of normal beta chains is beta thalassemia, a quantitative defect rather than an abnormal hemoglobin that polymerizes.
Ferric heme iron is methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen and causes cyanosis, not sickling.
Correct.

questions.stem: In a healthy kidney, the vasa recta carry away water reabsorbed in the medulla without washing out the medullary solute gradient. Which of the following features of the vasa recta allows this?
options: Rapid blood flow that clears solute before it can accumulate
Endothelium that is impermeable to both water and solute
Slow flow in hairpin loops allowing countercurrent exchange
Active sodium chloride pumping by the vasa recta endothelium
approach: Recall that the vasa recta are freely permeable to water and solute.
Follow blood down and back up the hairpin: it gains solute and loses water going down, then gives solute back and takes up water coming up.
Conclude that the hairpin shape and slow flow trap solute in the medulla while removing reabsorbed water.
questions.why: The vasa recta are passive exchangers. As blood descends into the hypertonic medulla, solute diffuses in and water moves out. As it rises back toward the cortex, solute diffuses out and water moves in. Because the loop turns back on itself, solute is handed from the ascending to the descending limb and stays in the medulla, and the slow flow limits washout. The net effect is removal of the water reabsorbed by the collecting ducts and loops with little loss of the gradient. The same arrangement short-circuits oxygen, which keeps medullary oxygen tension low and promotes sickling. When sickled cells block the vasa recta, the gradient is lost and urine cannot be concentrated.
whyNot: Rapid flow would wash solute out of the medulla and dissipate the gradient. Medullary blood flow is slow.
The vasa recta are freely permeable to water and solute. Their protective effect depends on passive exchange, not impermeability.
Correct.
The vasa recta do not pump salt. Active NaCl transport by the thick ascending limb is what builds the gradient.

topics: Countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta

questions.stem: His concentrating defect reflects loss of the nephrons whose long loops of Henle depend on the medullary vasa recta. His glomerular filtration rate, however, is preserved. Which of the following best explains why?
options: Most nephrons are juxtamedullary, with glomeruli spared from sickling
Most nephrons are cortical, supplied by peritubular capillaries
Cortical nephrons have long loops supplied by the vasa recta
Juxtamedullary glomeruli receive blood from the capsular arteries
approach: Separate the two nephron types: cortical nephrons with short loops and juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops and vasa recta.
Recall which type is more numerous: cortical nephrons, roughly four of every five.
Conclude that sickling in the medulla injures the few long-looped nephrons while the many cortical nephrons keep filtering.
questions.why: Most nephrons, roughly four out of five, are cortical nephrons. Their glomeruli sit in the outer cortex, their short loops reach only the outer medulla, and their efferent arterioles form peritubular capillaries in the well-oxygenated cortex, where flow is fast and sickling is uncommon. Juxtamedullary nephrons are fewer. Their glomeruli lie near the corticomedullary junction, their long loops reach the inner medulla, and their efferent arterioles form the vasa recta. These nephrons build the steep medullary gradient, so their loss impairs concentration while total GFR is largely kept. In sickle cell disease, GFR is often even higher than normal early on, which is why his creatinine is low.
whyNot: Juxtamedullary nephrons are the minority, and they are the ones injured here. They cannot account for preserved GFR.
Correct.
Cortical nephrons have short loops supplied by peritubular capillaries. Long loops with vasa recta belong to juxtamedullary nephrons.
All glomeruli receive blood from afferent arterioles that branch from cortical radiate arteries. Capsular vessels supply only the outer rim of the cortex.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl without sickle cell disease is evaluated for polyuria. Serum sodium is 133 mEq/L (135 to 145), and initial urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. After water restriction, urine osmolality rises to 680 mOsm/kg and does not rise further after desmopressin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary polydipsia
Central diabetes insipidus
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
approach: Note the low-normal serum sodium: water intake is driving the polyuria, rather than water loss.
Read the water deprivation result: urine concentrates well on its own, so ADH release and kidney response are intact.
Confirm with desmopressin: no further rise means her own ADH was already working.
questions.why: Polyuria with a slightly low serum sodium suggests excess water intake. When water is restricted, her own ADH is released and her kidneys concentrate urine to 680 mOsm/kg, and desmopressin adds nothing more, so both ADH secretion and the collecting duct response are intact. That is primary polydipsia. Long-standing high water intake can partly wash out the medullary gradient, so the maximum may be a bit below normal. In central diabetes insipidus, urine stays dilute with water restriction and rises sharply after desmopressin. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, urine stays dilute with both, and serum sodium tends to be high. The boy in this case cannot concentrate his urine for a related reason: sickling has destroyed the medullary gradient that ADH depends on.
whyNot: Correct.
Central diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine despite water restriction and a large rise after desmopressin, usually with a high-normal or high serum sodium.
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine that does not respond to water restriction or desmopressin. Her urine concentrated well.
SIADH causes hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and no polyuria. Her initial urine was maximally dilute.

dx: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with paraneoplastic polycythemia and hypercalcemia in a smoker
case: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 months of intermittent painless red urine, fatigue, and constipation. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and quit 3 years ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 78/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 146/88 mm Hg. A firm mass is palpable in the left flank. Hematocrit is 58% (41 to 53), serum calcium is 12.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5), and serum PTH is low. Arterial oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. CT shows a 9-cm enhancing mass in the left kidney with tumor extending into the left renal vein. Nephrectomy shows a golden-yellow tumor made of cells with clear cytoplasm. Diagnosis: clear cell renal cell carcinoma with paraneoplastic polycythemia and hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: Both copies of the VHL gene are inactivated in the tumor cells, and loss of VHL protein function contributes to his elevated hematocrit. In normal cells with adequate oxygen, which of the following is the function of this protein?
options: Targeting hydroxylated HIF for proteasomal degradation
Inactivating RAS by accelerating hydrolysis of its bound GTP
Holding E2F inactive until the cell is ready to enter S phase
Inhibiting mTOR growth signaling in a complex with hamartin
approach: Recall the VHL protein's partner: hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF).
Recall the normal pathway: with oxygen, HIF-alpha is hydroxylated, and VHL, part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, tags it for the proteasome.
Predict loss of VHL: HIF builds up even with normal oxygen and turns on VEGF and erythropoietin genes.
questions.why: When oxygen is plentiful, prolyl hydroxylases add hydroxyl groups to HIF-alpha. The VHL protein, part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, recognizes hydroxylated HIF and tags it with ubiquitin for destruction in the proteasome. In clear cell renal carcinoma, one VHL allele is usually lost with a deletion of chromosome 3p and the other is mutated or silenced. HIF then accumulates as if the cell were hypoxic and drives genes for VEGF (a highly vascular tumor), growth factors, glucose transporters, and erythropoietin. Tumor erythropoietin raises the red cell mass. A germline VHL mutation causes von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, with bilateral renal carcinomas, hemangioblastomas, and pheochromocytomas.
whyNot: Correct.
Accelerating RAS GTP hydrolysis is the role of neurofibromin, the NF1 gene product, not VHL.
Holding E2F inactive is the role of the RB protein in the G1 to S checkpoint.
Hamartin and tuberin, the TSC1 and TSC2 products, inhibit mTOR. Their loss causes angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis.

questions.stem: Biopsy of the tumor shows many infiltrating CD8+ T cells that recognize a mutated tumor protein made in the tumor cell cytoplasm. Which of the following best describes how these T cells recognize the tumor cells?
options: Peptides on MHC class II after endosomal processing
Intact tumor proteins bound directly by the T-cell receptor
Lipid antigens displayed on CD1d molecules
Peptides on MHC class I after proteasomal processing
approach: Note where the antigen is made: in the tumor cell cytoplasm, an endogenous protein.
Recall the pathway for endogenous proteins: proteasome, TAP transport into the endoplasmic reticulum, and loading onto MHC class I.
Match the T cell: CD8 binds MHC class I, so cytotoxic T cells see peptide on class I.
questions.why: Proteins made inside a cell, including mutated tumor proteins, are broken down by the proteasome. The peptides are carried into the endoplasmic reticulum by TAP, loaded onto MHC class I molecules, and displayed on the cell surface. Nearly all nucleated cells express MHC class I. CD8 binds class I, so cytotoxic T cells recognize the peptide-MHC complex with their T-cell receptor and kill the tumor cell with perforin and granzymes. Tumors escape by reducing MHC class I, which makes them targets for NK cells, or by expressing PD-L1, which switches off T cells through PD-1.
whyNot: MHC class II presents peptides from proteins taken up from outside the cell, mainly by antigen-presenting cells, and is recognized by CD4+ T cells.
T-cell receptors recognize processed peptides bound to MHC molecules. Intact proteins are recognized by antibodies and B-cell receptors.
CD1d presents lipid antigens to NKT cells, not protein peptides to CD8+ T cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: Red cell mass measurement confirms an increased red cell mass. After nephrectomy, his hematocrit falls to 45%. Which of the following best explains his preoperative hematocrit?
options: Hypoxemia from smoking-related chronic lung disease
Tumor production of erythropoietin
Acquired JAK2 mutation in marrow stem cells
Plasma volume loss from hypercalcemia-induced polyuria
approach: Confirm true polycythemia: the red cell mass is increased, so this is not just a low plasma volume.
Exclude hypoxic causes: his arterial oxygen saturation is normal.
Use the response to surgery: the hematocrit normalizes after the tumor is removed, so the tumor was the source of erythropoietin.
questions.why: Renal cell carcinoma can make erythropoietin, causing a secondary polycythemia with a normal arterial oxygen saturation and an inappropriately high erythropoietin level. Removing the tumor removes the source, and the hematocrit returns to normal. Other paraneoplastic effects of renal cell carcinoma include hypercalcemia from PTHrP, as in this patient with a low PTH, and hypertension from renin. The classic local triad is hematuria, flank pain, and a flank mass, though few patients have all three. The tumor spreads through the renal vein to the lungs and bones.
whyNot: Hypoxemia from lung disease would lower his oxygen saturation, which is 97%, and would not resolve after nephrectomy.
Correct.
A JAK2 mutation causes polycythemia vera, with low erythropoietin, and the hematocrit would not fall after nephrectomy.
Loss of plasma volume causes relative polycythemia with a normal red cell mass. His red cell mass is increased.

topics: Paraneoplastic syndromes of renal cell carcinoma

questions.stem: On CT, the tumor thrombus fills the left renal vein up to the point where the vein crosses the midline to enter the inferior vena cava. At that point, the vein lies between which of the following pairs of structures?
options: Celiac trunk in front and the abdominal aorta behind
Abdominal aorta in front and the lumbar vertebral body behind
Superior mesenteric artery in front and the aorta behind
Inferior mesenteric artery in front and the aorta behind
approach: Recall that the inferior vena cava lies to the right of the aorta, so the left renal vein must cross the midline.
Recall its path: in front of the aorta, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
Picture the angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, where the vein can be compressed.
questions.why: The inferior vena cava lies to the right of the aorta, so the left renal vein is longer than the right and must cross the midline. It passes anterior to the aorta and just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, through the angle between the two vessels. Compression in this angle is called the nutcracker phenomenon and can cause hematuria and a left varicocele. The left renal vein also receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. A tumor thrombus that blocks the vein can obstruct testicular drainage and cause a left varicocele that does not empty when the patient lies down.
whyNot: The celiac trunk arises higher, at about T12, above the level where the left renal vein crosses.
The left renal vein normally passes in front of the aorta. A vein running behind the aorta is an uncommon retroaortic variant.
Correct.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises lower, at about L3. It is the vessel that traps the isthmus of a horseshoe kidney.

dx: Uric acid nephrolithiasis in a man with gout
case: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of sudden severe right flank pain that comes in waves, with nausea. He has gout with recurrent attacks of podagra, obesity, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 104/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 148/90 mm Hg. Serum uric acid is 9.6 mg/dL (3.5 to 7.2), and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urine pH is 5.0 (4.5 to 8.0), and urinalysis shows red blood cells and yellow-brown rhomboid crystals. An abdominal x-ray shows no calcification, but noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm stone in the right proximal ureter with mild hydronephrosis. Diagnosis: uric acid nephrolithiasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his urine pH of 5.0 favors formation of this type of stone?
options: Acid urine lets bacterial urease generate more ammonium
Acid urine converts uric acid into an insoluble urate salt
More urate is protonated to poorly soluble uric acid
Acid urine lowers the solubility of calcium phosphate
approach: Recall the acid-base chemistry: uric acid has a pKa of about 5.5.
Apply it: below the pKa, most of it is in the protonated uric acid form; above it, most is the ionized urate salt.
Recall solubility: uric acid is far less soluble than urate, so acid urine lets it crystallize.
questions.why: Uric acid is a weak acid with a pKa of about 5.5. In urine more alkaline than that, most of it exists as ionized urate, which is fairly soluble. In urine more acidic than that, most of it is protonated to uric acid, which is poorly soluble and crystallizes. Persistently acidic urine is the main driver of uric acid stones, more than the amount of uric acid excreted. Risk factors include gout, insulin resistance and the metabolic syndrome, tumor lysis, and high purine intake. These stones are radiolucent on plain x-rays but visible on CT, and alkalinizing the urine can dissolve them.
whyNot: Urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus make the urine alkaline and form struvite stones. They do not act in acid urine.
This reverses the chemistry. Acid urine shifts urate toward the uric acid form, and the ionized salt is the more soluble one.
Correct.
Calcium phosphate is less soluble in alkaline urine, as in distal renal tubular acidosis. Acid urine does not favor it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his pain comes in waves?
options: Inflammation of the parietal peritoneum over the ureter
Ureteral peristalsis against the obstructing stone
Ischemic necrosis of the renal papillae
Irritation of somatic nerves in the abdominal wall
approach: Identify the problem: a stone blocking the proximal ureter, with dilation above it.
Recall what the ureter does: smooth muscle peristalsis pushes urine toward the bladder.
Conclude that each contraction against the stone raises pressure and stretch, producing waves of visceral pain.
questions.why: Renal colic comes from an obstructing stone. Urine backs up above the stone, the ureter dilates, and its smooth muscle keeps contracting in peristaltic waves against the blockage. Each contraction raises the pressure and stretch in the ureter and renal pelvis, triggering visceral pain that comes and goes, often with nausea and hematuria. Persistent obstruction leads to hydronephrosis, and stagnant urine above the stone can become infected, which is an emergency.
whyNot: Peritoneal irritation causes steady, well-localized pain that worsens with movement. Renal colic is visceral and colicky, and patients often cannot lie still.
Correct.
Papillary necrosis can cause colic when a sloughed papilla passes, but this patient has a uric acid stone, not papillary necrosis.
Somatic nerve irritation causes sharp, well-localized, constant pain. Visceral ureteral pain is poorly localized and comes in waves.

questions.stem: Many patients with uric acid stones and insulin resistance, like this man, excrete less ammonium than normal. Which of the following best explains why low ammonium excretion makes the urine more acidic?
options: Less filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed by the proximal tubule
More bicarbonate is secreted by beta-intercalated cells
Less hydrogen ion is secreted through proximal Na+/H+ exchange
Less NH3 is available to buffer secreted hydrogen ions
approach: Recall how the kidney excretes acid: secreted hydrogen ions are bound by buffers, mainly phosphate (titratable acid) and NH3, which forms NH4+.
Recall the advantage of NH3: it traps hydrogen ions as NH4+, so large amounts of acid leave without lowering urine pH much.
Predict that with less NH3, more of the secreted hydrogen ions stay free, so urine pH falls.
questions.why: The proximal tubule makes ammonium from glutamine, and each ammonium excreted adds a new bicarbonate to the blood. In the collecting duct, NH3 diffuses into the lumen and binds secreted hydrogen ions to form NH4+, which is charged and trapped in the urine. This lets the kidney excrete most of the daily acid load without a large drop in urine pH. Phosphate (titratable acid) has a limited capacity. When ammonium production is low, as is thought to occur with insulin resistance, more of the secreted hydrogen ions remain free and urine pH falls, often below 5.5. That favors uric acid crystallization.
whyNot: Reclaiming less filtered bicarbonate leaves more bicarbonate in the urine, which raises urine pH.
Bicarbonate secretion by beta-intercalated cells raises urine pH, as in metabolic alkalosis.
Less proximal hydrogen ion secretion leaves bicarbonate unreclaimed and raises urine pH, as in proximal renal tubular acidosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two days later, the stone has moved to the distal ureter just above the bladder, and his pain is now felt in the right groin rather than the flank. Which of the following best explains this change in where the pain is felt?
options: Distal ureteral afferents enter cord segments that supply the groin
The stone compresses the obturator nerve where it runs on the pelvic wall
The stone compresses the femoral nerve as it passes along the iliacus
Somatic pain fibers from the distal ureter travel in the pudendal nerve
approach: Recall that ureteral pain fibers are visceral afferents that run with sympathetic nerves to about T11 to L2.
Recall referred pain: the brain assigns visceral pain to the skin supplied by the same cord segments.
Apply it: the upper ureter projects to higher segments (flank), and the lower ureter projects to lower segments around L1 (groin).
questions.why: Visceral afferents from the ureter travel with sympathetic fibers to the spinal cord at about T11 to L2. Pain is referred to the skin supplied by the same segments, because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same dorsal horn neurons. The upper ureter enters higher segments, so a stone there causes flank pain. As the stone moves down, the pain moves with it toward the lower segments, around L1, and is felt in the groin and sometimes the scrotum or labia. Pain shifting from flank to groin tracks the stone's descent.
whyNot: Correct.
Compression of the obturator nerve would cause pain and numbness on the inner thigh with weak hip adduction. A ureteral stone does not compress it.
The femoral nerve lies outside the ureter's path and its compression would cause anterior thigh numbness and quadriceps weakness, not groin colic.
The ureter has no somatic innervation. Its pain fibers are visceral afferents traveling with sympathetic nerves.

dx: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome from a complement factor H mutation
case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of fatigue, decreased urine output, and pallor. One week earlier she had a mild upper respiratory infection. She has had no diarrhea. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse 104/min, respirations 18/min, and blood pressure 172/104 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), and platelet count is 42,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000). The blood smear shows schistocytes. Serum LDH is 1,240 U/L (100 to 250), haptoglobin is undetectable, and creatinine is 4.2 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). The direct antiglobulin test is negative. ADAMTS13 activity is 72% (normal over 60%). Stool testing for Shiga toxin is negative. Serum C3 is 58 mg/dL (90 to 180). Genetic testing shows a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the complement factor H gene. Diagnosis: atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the endothelial injury in this patient?
options: A toxin that enters endothelial cells and halts protein synthesis
Ultralarge von Willebrand factor multimers that are not cleaved
IgG antibodies against complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4
Unchecked alternative complement activation on endothelial cells
approach: Note what is excluded: no diarrhea and no Shiga toxin, and ADAMTS13 activity is normal.
Recall the role of factor H: it protects host cells from the alternative complement pathway.
Conclude that loss of factor H lets complement attack glomerular endothelium after a trigger such as an infection.
questions.why: Factor H is a plasma protein that binds C3b on host cell surfaces, speeds the breakdown of the alternative pathway C3 convertase, and serves as a cofactor for factor I. With one defective copy, a trigger such as an infection or pregnancy lets the alternative pathway run unchecked on endothelial cells, especially in the glomeruli. The membrane attack complex damages the endothelium, platelets and fibrin form microthrombi, and the result is microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Typical hemolytic uremic syndrome follows bloody diarrhea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7, while TTP results from ADAMTS13 deficiency. Atypical disease is treated by blocking C5.
whyNot: Shiga toxin enters endothelial cells and stops protein synthesis in typical hemolytic uremic syndrome. She had no diarrhea and no Shiga toxin.
Uncleaved ultralarge von Willebrand factor multimers cause TTP from ADAMTS13 deficiency. Her ADAMTS13 activity is normal.
Antibodies to heparin and platelet factor 4 cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs prior heparin exposure and does not cause schistocytes with renal failure.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her hemolysis resolves with treatment, but she is left with chronic kidney disease, with a creatinine of 2.8 mg/dL. Six months later, her hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL. Which of the following sets of findings would best indicate that her anemia now results from loss of kidney tissue rather than ongoing hemolysis?
options: Normal MCV, low reticulocyte count, and no schistocytes
Normal MCV, high reticulocyte count, and many schistocytes
Low MCV, low serum ferritin, and pencil-shaped red cells
High MCV, low reticulocyte count, and hypersegmented neutrophils
approach: Recall where erythropoietin comes from: peritubular interstitial cells in the kidney that respond to hypoxia.
Predict the anemia when those cells are lost: too little erythropoietin, so the marrow makes too few normal-sized red cells.
Contrast hemolysis: the marrow responds with many reticulocytes, and a microangiopathy shows schistocytes.
questions.why: Erythropoietin is made by fibroblast-like interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries. Low oxygen stabilizes HIF, which turns on the erythropoietin gene. In chronic kidney disease these cells are lost, erythropoietin stays inappropriately low for the degree of anemia, and the marrow makes too few red cells. The result is a normocytic, normochromic anemia with a low reticulocyte count. Ongoing thrombotic microangiopathy would instead show a brisk reticulocyte response, schistocytes, and a high LDH.
whyNot: Correct.
A high reticulocyte count with schistocytes means the marrow is responding to ongoing red cell destruction, which is active microangiopathy.
A low MCV with low ferritin and pencil cells is iron deficiency anemia.
A high MCV with hypersegmented neutrophils points to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

questions.stem: Fibrin and platelet thrombi occlude many of her afferent arterioles. Which of the following best explains why the tubules of the affected nephrons also become ischemic?
options: Tubules are supplied by branches of the interlobar veins
Peritubular capillaries arise directly from the arcuate arteries
Peritubular capillaries arise from the efferent arterioles
Tubules receive blood from capsular arteries of the kidney
approach: Trace the renal arterial path: renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate, cortical radiate, then afferent arteriole.
Recall the two capillary beds in series: the glomerulus, then the efferent arteriole, then the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
Conclude that blocking the afferent arteriole cuts off both beds.
questions.why: Renal blood flows from the renal artery through segmental, interlobar, arcuate, and cortical radiate arteries to the afferent arterioles. Each afferent arteriole feeds a glomerulus, and the blood then leaves through the efferent arteriole into a second capillary bed: peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules, or vasa recta in the medulla for juxtamedullary nephrons. Blood then returns through the renal veins. Because the two capillary beds lie in series, a thrombus in the afferent arteriole starves both the glomerulus and the tubules downstream, which is why severe thrombotic microangiopathy can cause tubular injury and cortical necrosis.
whyNot: Veins carry blood away from the kidney tissue. Tubules are supplied by capillaries arising from efferent arterioles.
Arcuate arteries give off cortical radiate arteries and then afferent arterioles. They do not feed peritubular capillaries directly.
Correct.
Capsular vessels supply only a thin outer rim of cortex. Most tubules depend on blood that has already passed through the glomerulus.

questions.stem: Her hypertension reflects impaired sodium excretion by her injured kidneys. By contrast, a patient with an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma and normal kidneys develops hypertension and hypokalemia but no edema. Which of the following best explains the absence of edema in that patient?
options: Mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct are lost over time
Higher arterial pressure raises renal sodium excretion
Suppressed renin lowers aldosterone back into the normal range
Increased ADH secretion promotes excretion of free water
approach: Recall that excess aldosterone first causes sodium and water retention and a rise in blood pressure.
Apply pressure natriuresis: higher renal perfusion pressure increases sodium and water excretion.
Conclude that sodium balance is restored at a higher blood pressure, so edema does not develop but hypertension persists.
questions.why: Over the long term, arterial pressure is set by the kidney's pressure natriuresis: when arterial pressure rises, the kidneys excrete more sodium and water. In primary hyperaldosteronism, the extra aldosterone first causes sodium retention and volume expansion. Blood pressure rises, pressure natriuresis increases sodium excretion, and intake and output come back into balance at a higher pressure. This escape from sodium retention prevents edema, while hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin persist. When the kidneys are injured, as in this patient, they need a much higher pressure to excrete the same sodium, and volume overload develops more easily.
whyNot: Mineralocorticoid receptors are not lost. Potassium secretion and hypokalemia continue, showing the receptors are still active.
Correct.
In primary hyperaldosteronism, the adenoma secretes aldosterone on its own, so low renin does not lower aldosterone.
ADH reduces free water excretion. It does not remove the extra sodium and water that would cause edema.
